messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Preliminary IO Validation in Nomad
parts:
Here's an example of what a function implementation looks like,

  template <short AutodiffOrder, bool StrictSmoothness, bool ValidateIO>

  inline var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>

    sqrt(const var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>& input) {

    

    // Validate inputs

    if (ValidateIO) {

      double val = input.first_val();

      validate_input(val, "sqrt");

      validate_lower_bound(val, 0, "sqrt");

    }

      

    // Expand expression graph

    const short partials_order = 3;  // Explicit instantiation for readability only

    const unsigned int n_inputs = 1; // Ditto

    

    create_node<unary_var_node<AutodiffOrder, partials_order>>(n_inputs);


    // Push value

    double val = std::sqrt(input.first_val());

    

    try {

      push_dual_numbers<AutodiffOrder, ValidateIO>(val);

    } catch(nomad_error& e) {

      throw nomad_output_value_error("sqrt");

    }

    

    // Push input edges

    push_inputs(input.dual_numbers());

    

    // Push partials

    double d2 = 1.0 / input.first_val();

    

    try {

      if (AutodiffOrder >= 1) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= 0.5 * d2);

      if (AutodiffOrder >= 2) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= - 0.5 * d2);

      if (AutodiffOrder >= 3) push_partials<ValidateIO>(val *= - 1.5 * d2);

    } catch(nomad_error& e) {

      throw nomad_output_partial_error("sqrt");

    }


    return var<AutodiffOrder, StrictSmoothness, ValidateIO>(next_node_idx_ - 1);

    

  }


Ultimately the function implementation look really clean except for all of the validation stuff, but that's as clean as I could get the checks while also being able to disable them.


Anyone have any thoughts or alternative suggestions?


Everything is working and I just need to finish implementing the output validation and testing framework.  The cleaner code also seems to lead to faster execution (Clang 3.6 is great!).  Next comes basic matrix support and then vectorization, I guess?  Probably a readable manual would help, too.  Ugh.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Preliminary IO Validation in Nomad
parts:
Not so much vertical space? :-)

What does validate_input do?

So the idea is that people write code that's templated on
the outside with order, smoothness and validation, then you
invoke it however you want?

Does the explicit instantiation for partials and n_inputs
slow anything down? I don't know how well the compiler can
inline non-static const values.

Do you really need to do the try/catch in the evaluation of
sqrt? I'd think that'd really slow things down. Why doesn't
the function itself just throw? What can sqrt() do to recover
from its own errors? Asked another way around, when do the
functions called inside the try ever throw? I'd think it'd
only be internal memory issues. You don't want to try to
catch coding errors this way. Maybe the try/catch can be
part of ValidateIO? But that'd really clutter up the interface.

- Bob

What does validate_input do?

Checks for nan, throws if necessary,

  inline void validate_input(double val, std::string f_name) {

    std::cout << "Trying to validate input value " << val << std::endl;

    if (unlikely(std::isnan(val))) throw nomad_input_error(f_name);

    else return;

  }

So the idea is that people write code that's templated on
the outside with order, smoothness and validation, then you
invoke it however you want?

People write functors templated against a var type; when you want to instantiate
a  functor you can set order, smoothness, and validation yourself or use one of
the fine typedefs that keep everything hidden away.

Does the explicit instantiation for partials and n_inputs
slow anything down?  I don't know how well the compiler can
inline non-static const values.

Not that I can tell but we can always go through and remove them if someone
can detect a nontrivial difference.

Do you really need to do the try/catch in the evaluation of
sqrt?  I'd think that'd really slow things down.  Why doesn't
the function itself just throw?  What can sqrt() do to recover
from its own errors?  Asked another way around, when do the
functions called inside the try ever throw?  I'd think it'd
only be internal memory issues.  You don't want to try to
catch coding errors this way.  Maybe the try/catch can be
part of ValidateIO?  But that'd really clutter up the interface.

Ah, sorry, I didn't describe this thoroughly.  The try block is to catch exceptions
thrown from push_dual_numbers and push_partials which will check for NaNs
upon request (via the ValidateIO template parameter).  This allows us to immediately
identify where the NaN first arises (push_dual_numbers and push_partials wrapped
separately to be able to distinguish the two).
